Family history · Schaal–Glaudell line · Prime 6 Illinois 1913 — Hollywood, Florida 1990

Adeline Schaal
The Girl from Bonfield

↑² MF— paternal grandmother of Dana (the anchor of this page)Proven

Adeline Rosella Emma Minnie Schaal was born on 13 October 1913 in Illinois, the daughter of Frank Schaal and Edith Schultz. In 1934 she married Noble Glaudell and had two sons, Noble Lee and Donald Ray; the marriage ended, and in 1942 she married Oliver Sutton, with whom she later moved to Florida. Widowed in 1970, she married Henry Istock in 1973. She died in Hollywood, Florida, on 10 September 1990, and is buried at Mount Emblem Cemetery in Elmhurst, Illinois.

§1 The girl from Bonfield

She was given names enough for three girls, and a birthplace two counties still argue over.

Adeline Rosella Emma Minnie Schaal24 was born 13 October 19131 Proven. Where she was born is not settled: the family tree says Bonfield, in Kankakee County; her FamilySearch page says Wilton Center, over the line in Will County Disputed2.

She was a daughter of the German Lutheran farm country northwest of Kankakee — her father's Schaal people and her mother's Schultz people had farmed Kankakee and Will counties since the 1860s325. Her girlhood is nearly paperless: two photographs and a class ring are what survive of it before the census speaks in 1930.

§2 The census trail

Three enumerations caught her — a daughter in her father's house, a young wife in Elwood, a wife again in Chicago. The fourth, when she was six, has never been found.

1920 — NOT LOCATEDShe was 6

No 1920 appearance of Adeline, or of Frank and Edith's household with her in it, has been located anywhere in the lane's work. It is the one unfinished pull of her census trail. Open

1930 — Custer Township, Will CountyED 98-5 · sheet 4A · 15 Apr 1930

Frank Schaal, 51, a railroad labourer who owned his $1,100 home; his wife Edith, 45; Frank Jr., 28; Adeline, 16; Leslie, 13. Against Adeline's name the relationship column reads, in full: Daughter. Proven4

1940 — Elwood, Will CountyED 99-16 · sheet 3B

Noble Glaudell, head; his wife entered as "Areline Glandell," 26; sons Noble, 5, and Donald, 3; a rented house. The household had lived at Elwood since 1935. Proven5

1950 — Chicago, Cook CountyED 103-3711 · p. 7 · House No. 494

Oliver Sutton, 51, a carpenter in construction, head; Adeline, 36, entered as WIFE; and the boys under their stepfather's surname — "Nobel Sutton," 15, and Donald Sutton, 13. The sheet records no street name, only the house number 494. Proven6

§3 The Glaudell marriage

She was twenty when she married Noble Glaudell, and a mother by the summer.

On 18 January 1934 Adeline married Noble Glaudell at Crown Point, Lake County, Indiana — the county seat just over the state line; the license was issued by George W. Sweigart, Clerk of the Lake Circuit Court, and the Rev. August Biester married them the same day Proven7. Their first son, Noble Lee, was born 24 July 19348.

That spring the family took the baby home to Bonfield: the register of Zion Lutheran Church records his baptism on 7 April 1935, in the parsonage, naming the parents "Mr. Noble Glaudell and his wife Adeline nee Schaal," with her father among the sponsors — and her sister Irene baptized her own son in the entry directly above, the same day9. A second son, Donald Ray, was born 12 October 1936 at Elwood1026. By 1940 the census shows the young family at Elwood (§2). In October 1940 Noble's draft card still named Adeline as his wife and contact11. It is the last record that shows the marriage intact.

What is not in hand

No wedding photograph of Adeline and Noble is known to survive, and no record yet read documents the marriage's everyday years — the Elwood addresses, the work, the rooms. The chapter stands on a license, a baptism, a census sheet, and a draft card.

§4 The parting

No divorce decree has ever been found; the parting has to be told from the edges of other people's paperwork.

The bracket is tight. In October 1940 Noble's draft card names Adeline as his wife. On 18 March 1942 she married Oliver Sutton in Chicago. And when Noble enlisted on 23 October 1942, his Army record described him as divorced, with dependents. The marriage therefore ended in law somewhere between October 1940 and March 1942 — sixteen months hold the whole parting, and no document in hand narrows it further Probable12. The boys stayed with her: the 1950 census finds both in her Chicago household (§2).

§5 Chicago

The second marriage is proven twice over — by its license in 1942 and by its household in 1950 — and its texture is bowling.

Oliver Evan Sutton was an Indiana man, born 7 December 1897 at Westport, Decatur County, the son of Francis M. Sutton and Ida Bell Sutton of Sand Creek13. Adeline married him on 18 March 1942 in Chicago, Cook County — marriage license 1723309 Proven14. The 1950 household stands at §2.

What fills the Chicago years in her file is a league: sponsored women's bowling teams, season after season — a dark-kit team in a knotty-pine room (ADE-003), a Garberson's Drugs team (ADE-009), and a Pete's Pizzeria team photographed in 1959 (ADE-012, ADE-013). The alley is named in the family's own file descriptions: Grand Bowl, on Grand Avenue in Franklin Park15.

The sponsor thread, honestly unresolved

No document found in the 1949–1956 archives ties a Pete's Pizzeria to her team. The strongest candidate — Pete's Pizza at Belmont and Western in Chicago, founded 1955 — fits on name and dates alone, and the 1959 photographs sit comfortably inside its life; that is a candidate, not an identification. Garberson's Drugs left nothing but its sign: no directory, dataset, or archive entry for the store has been found. Grand Bowl itself is gone — closed in the early 2000s, its building now a church; the address 9777 Grand Avenue is a strong candidate for its site, unproven.16

§6 South

After the 1950 sheet, the record goes quiet for nineteen years; when it speaks again, she is a Floridian.

When her mother Edith died on 15 July 1969 at Monticello, Illinois, the Decatur Daily Review named among her survivors "Mrs. Adeline Sutton, Hollywood, Fla." — so by the summer of 1969 Adeline was in Florida, and still a Sutton Probable17. When she moved south, and whether she and Oliver went together, no record in hand says. Oliver died at Hollywood on 6 February 197018. She was fifty-six, a widow for the first time.

§7 Hollywood

She kept the Sutton name three more years, then took a fourth name for the rest of her life.

On 26 January 1973, in Broward County, Adeline Rosella Sutton, maiden name Schaal, married Henry Istock — Florida Marriage Certificate 000677 Proven19. She was fifty-nine. She had been Schaal for twenty years, Glaudell for eight, Sutton for thirty-one; she would be Istock for seventeen, the rest of her life. The studio sittings with Henry belong to these years.

In 1981 she went home for the Wilmington High School class of 1931's27 fiftieth reunion. Henry Istock died before her: he was interred at Fred Hunter's in Hollywood on 26 March 1990, and the cemetery's records name Adeline as the OWNER of his burial space20.

Adeline died at Hollywood on 10 September 1990, aged seventy-six, under the name Adeline Istock Proven21. Her funeral was held that September in Hollywood, with arrangements by Fred Hunter's Hollywood Memorial Gardens Home, named in her Sun Sentinel obituary of 12 September 199022. She is not buried in Florida. She lies at Mount Emblem Cemetery in Elmhurst, Illinois — Section Twilight, Lot 1102, Grave 2, beside Oliver Sutton in Grave 1 Proven23.

The proof trail

Her open questions are not mysteries; they are unread records, unmailed letters, and one unwritten correction. Each below names the instrument that answers it.

One word: Daughter

For years no record named Adeline with a parent. The 1930 Custer Township sheet, read at image grade in October 2026, writes "Daughter" against her name in Frank Schaal's household; and Edith Schaal's 1969 obituary names "Mrs. Adeline Sutton, Hollywood, Fla." among her daughters. Two independent primary records: the parentage rests.

Where was the first wedding?

Her first marriage was long carried as Point Township, Posey County, Indiana, on a FamilySearch citation no one had read at image grade. Her lane holds the license itself — Lake County Marriage Records 1933–34, Crown Point, the Rev. August Biester — and this page follows the record that has been seen; the Posey citation stands as a disputed row in the ledger, not as fact.

The burial that wasn't in Florida

Her Find a Grave memorial placed her burial at Fred Hunter's in Hollywood — a misreading: Fred Hunter's was the funeral home named in her obituary, not her burial place. Mount Emblem Cemetery confirmed her interment at Elmhurst when the family asked, plot and all; the family knew she was there. The memorial's error still stands online; the correction is an exact, written proposal that fires on the family's word.28

A house number with no street

The 1950 sheet gives House No. 494 and no street. Until the street is known, the Cook County deed pass and the Chicago Sanborn pass for her Sutton home have nothing to aim at; the widened neighbor sweep of that district is the likeliest route to it.

The sponsor thread

See §5's finding box: the Pete's identification rests on name and dates, Garberson's on a sign alone. The instruments that could settle them are named in the footnotes — directory listings and the paywalled league pages of the 1950s Chicago papers.

Open questions

  1. "Was she born at Bonfield or at Wilton Center?" — Her 1913 baptism, most likely in the register of Zion Lutheran Church, Bonfield; the transcription book (Kankakee Valley Genealogical Society, 2006) or the church itself. The family's ask letter stands drafted, unsent.
  2. "Where was she in 1920?" — One sheet of the 1920 census, Frank and Edith's household with a six-year-old Adeline in it; the pull is queued with its pullspec.
  3. "Where is the divorce decree?" — A court record in Will County, Cook County, or Lake County, Indiana, between October 1940 and March 1942; no court has yet been tested.
  4. "What street was House No. 494 on?" — The widened neighbor sweep of Chicago ED 103-3711, or a Cook County deed for the Sutton years.
  5. "Who was Frank Schaal's father?" — The Kankakee Public Library marriage return for Frank × Edith, re-sent 19 October 2026 and awaited; the Zion register session behind it.
  6. "What were Henry Istock's dates?" — His death record, and Fred Hunter's purchase record for his burial space, which holds his widow's address, birthdate, and name as its owner; the follow-up letter is sent and awaited.
  7. "Which Pete's was it — and who was 'Capt. L..'?" — A 1950s Chicago directory listing for the sponsor, the league pages of the Chicago papers, and the family's knowledge of the team captain.
  8. "Which woman is Adeline?" — In the 1944 zoo photograph (ADE-024) the family is asked to place her by the two anchors in the frame — the dark beaded necklace and the envelope clutch; and the twelve at Grandma Jackson's table (ADE-027) await names.
